```{r setup}
library(isoniche)
```

This vignette explains what **isoniche** computes. The method is described
in full by Granot, Dubiner & Belmaker (2026).

## Isodars

Under density-dependent habitat selection, individuals settle where their
expected fitness is highest. As a habitat fills up, its quality declines, so
later individuals settle in the next-best habitat (the ideal free
distribution; Fretwell & Lucas 1969). The densities in two habitats at
which fitness is equal form a line, the *isodar* (Morris 1987):

$$N_2 = a + b N_1 .$$

The intercept $a$ measures a density-independent preference: habitat 2 holds
$a$ individuals before habitat 1 receives any. The slope $b$ measures how
quickly habitat 2 fills compared with habitat 1 as total abundance rises. A
species without habitat preference has $a = 0$ and $b = 1$.

Isodars are estimated from replicates (sites, or surveys) in which the
species' densities in each habitat are known. Because both densities are
measured with error, they are fitted by total least squares (major-axis
regression), not by ordinary regression.

## Why abundance-based indices are biased

Whenever an intercept is not zero, the share of individuals in each habitat
changes with total abundance. A rare species keeps most individuals in its
preferred habitat and looks like a specialist; the same species, when
abundant, spills into other habitats and looks like a generalist. A classic
index, such as 1 - Gini of the habitat proportions, therefore partly
measures abundance:

```{r bias, fig.height = 3.5}
set.seed(2)
sim <- simulate_isodars(slope1 = 1, slope2 = 1, int1 = 8, int2 = 8, noise = 1,
                        n = 60)
classic <- apply(as.matrix(sim[1:3]), 1, function(x) {
  x <- sort(x)
  n <- length(x)
  g <- 2 * sum(seq_len(n) * x) / (n * sum(x)) - (n + 1) / n
  (1 - g - 1 / n) * n / (n - 1)
})
plot(sim$total_abundance, classic, log = "x", pch = 19,
     xlab = "Total abundance at the site",
     ylab = "Classic niche breadth (1 - Gini)")
```

All sites come from one species with fixed habitat preferences, yet niche
breadth rises with abundance. Rarefaction (Cayuela et al. 2015) removes the
effect of sample size on observed habitat use, but not this effect, which
is part of how the species uses habitats.

## Pairwise isodars and the n-dimensional isodar

With $H$ habitats there are $H(H-1)/2$ pairwise isodars, fitted separately,
each with every site at which both habitats were sampled. The examples use
three species of `moorea_fish`, reef fish counts from Moorea (BioTIME 2.0;
Dornelas et al. 2025), as in the paper:

```{r pairwise}
three <- c("Acanthurus nigrofuscus", "Scarus schlegeli", "Siganus argenteus")
fish3 <- moorea_fish[moorea_fish$species %in% three, ]
pw <- fit_isodars(fish3, species = "species", site = "site",
                  habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance")
pw$fit[[1]]
```

The n-dimensional isodar is a *line* through habitat space, not a plane.
Equal fitness in $H$ habitats imposes $H - 1$ equalities, leaving one degree
of freedom: as total abundance changes, densities in all habitats move
together along one line. Its direction says how fast each habitat fills as
abundance rises (the analogue of the slopes), and where it enters each
habitat reflects density-independent preferences (the analogue of the
intercepts). The line is the first principal axis of the site x habitat
densities; `var_explained` is the share of variance it accounts for.

```{r line}
ln <- fit_isodars(fish3, species = "species", site = "site",
                  habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance", dim = "ndim")
ln$fit[[3]]
```

When some sites lack some habitats, the line is estimated with a one-factor
model that uses every site with at least two habitats (`ndim_method =
"latent"`, fitted with **glmmTMB**).

## The isodar-adjusted inequality

The *isodar-adjusted inequality* (IAI) allocates a chosen total abundance
$T$ among habitats as the isodars predict, and computes 1 - Gini of that
allocation, scaled to 0-1. For pairwise isodars the allocation solves the
isodar equations $N_j - b N_i = a$ by weighted least squares subject to
$\sum N = T$; habitats predicted negative are set to 0 and the rest
re-solved. By default each isodar is weighted by its inverse variance,
$1 / (sd^2 (1 + b^2))$ (`weights = "1/var"`). For the line, the allocation
is the point where the line meets $\sum N = T$.

Two values summarise the IAI:

* **DI niche breadth**, at the *spillover abundance* $T_0$: the smallest
  total at which every used habitat holds at least one individual (per
  reference effort). It mainly reflects the intercepts.
* **DD niche breadth**, as $T \to \infty$, where only the slopes (the
  direction of the line) matter.

```{r nb}
nb <- niche_breadth(fish3, species = "species", site = "site",
                    habitat = "habitat", abundance = "abundance",
                    n_boot = 199, seed = 1)
nb[c("species", "nb_di", "nb_di_lower", "nb_di_upper", "spillover_abundance",
     "nb_dd", "nb_dd_lower", "nb_dd_upper")]
```

Intervals come from resampling whole sites with replacement and refitting
the isodars. The density-dependent value can also be computed at a given
total (`dependent_at = 1000`, as in the paper) or at the largest observed
site total (`dependent_at = "max_observed"`).

## The niche breadth curve

Above $T_0$, until a habitat is clipped to zero, the allocation is linear in
$T$. If, in addition, no two habitats swap rank anywhere above $T_0$,
$$NB(T) = NB_{DD} + (NB_{DI} - NB_{DD}) \frac{T_0}{T},$$
so niche breadth is halfway between the two values at $T = 2T_0$. Where the
predicted abundances of two habitats cross, the curve changes course (it
keeps the form $A + B/T$, with new constants, between crossings); these
*preference reversals* are reported, as are habitats used at low density and
abandoned at high density:

```{r reversals}
nb$abandoned
nb$reversals[[1]]
```

```{r curve, fig.height = 5}
curve <- iai_curve(ln, n_boot = 99, seed = 1)
plot(curve, abundances = 1000, crossings = TRUE)
```

Plotting against abundance relative to $T_0$ puts all DI values at 1:

```{r curve-relative, fig.height = 5}
plot(curve, x_axis = "relative")
```

## Indices from isodar parameters (Appendix S1)

`pairwise_niche()` summarises the pairwise isodars directly. An isodar can
be written with either habitat on the x-axis, so the indices are built to
give the same answer either way: slopes enter as $(\log b)^2$, because
$\log(1/b) = -\log b$, and intercepts as the perpendicular distance of the
isodar from the origin, $d = |a| / \sqrt{1 + b^2}$. The indices are the
inverse root-mean-square deviations from no preference,
$1 / \sqrt{\sum w (\log b)^2 / \sum w}$ for slopes and
$1 / \sqrt{\sum w d^2 / \sum w}$ for intercepts, and the weighted means of
$|\log b|$ and $d$. The intercept index is in abundance units, so it
depends on effort; the slope index does not.

```{r appendix}
pn <- pairwise_niche(pw$fit[[1]], weights = "1/var")
pn
```

The isodars of three habitats should agree with each other: going round
the cycle A to B to C and back to A, the slopes multiply to 1. `$cycles`
gives this product for every set of three habitats, and flags it when it
departs from 1 by more than a factor of `exp(cycle_tolerance)` (default
1.5):

```{r cycles}
pn$cycles
```

The earlier, orientation-dependent indices (mean intercept and slope,
deviations $(b - 1)^2$ and $a^2$) are available with `scale = "linear"`.

## Simulating data

`simulate_isodars()` generates densities in any number of habitats from
known isodars, optionally with missing habitats, which is useful for
checking the method on a known answer:

```{r simulate}
set.seed(4)
sim <- simulate_isodars(2, 2, 0, 0, noise = 0.5, n = 60)
iai(fit_isodars(sim, hab_cols = c("hab1", "hab2", "hab3"), dim = "ndim"),
    abundances = 100)
```

The true value for these isodars is 0.571.
